findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Garden Street, St Annes is contractually due for completion on 28 October 2026, with a latest budget of £1.295m and £656k spent to 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the scheme forms part of a linked programme with Pier Link and Orchard Road, and that it is expected to complete within budget. It does not report whether completion has taken place.
findings.matters: A contract completion date that falls before the meeting is a deadline the reader will want confirmed as met or missed.
findings.figures: £1.295m latest budget (£1,000k approved plus £295k slippage); £656k actual expenditure to 30 September 2026; £639k variance (FAV)
findings.quote: This project is contractually due for completion on the 28th October 2026

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Executive Committee approved a retrospective, fully funded addition of £86,284 to the capital programme for St Annes Promenade Paddling Pool remedial works.
findings.detail: The paper says the addition is funded from the Capital Investment Reserve and that the scheme is on target for completion in 2026/27. The addition was approved in September 2026.
findings.matters: A capital addition approved after the spend had started is a governance point, and it draws on the Capital Investment Reserve.
findings.figures: £86,284 retrospective addition; £86k latest budget; £76k actual expenditure to 30 September 2026
findings.quote: Executive Committee in Sept 26 approved a retrospective fully funded addition of £86,284 to the Council’s Capital Programme

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants are expected to underspend by approx £400k at year end, against a £2.328m budget.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the expected underspend to competitive contractor pricing and lower-value grants. It notes that the Better Care Fund grant for 2026/27 is £1.535m, and total budget includes £713k slipped from 2025/26.
findings.matters: An expected underspend on a grant-funded programme of this size indicates how much Better Care Fund money may be returned or carried over.
findings.figures: £2.328m total budget including £713k slippage; £657k actual expenditure to 30 September 2026; £1.535m Better Care Fund grant 2026/27; approx £400k expected year-end underspend
findings.quote: It is expected there will be an underspend at year end of approx £400k.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: St Annes Square Public Realm Improvements (Phase 1) was delivered under budget, with a committee report to follow on transferring the unspent £178k.
findings.detail: The paper says the scheme is contractually complete and in the defects period, with retention and professional fees still to be paid. It says a report will ask committee to approve transferring the unspent capital to the Pier Link and Garden Street schemes.
findings.matters: A scheme that completed with an underspend and a proposal to reallocate it is a reallocation decision other councils managing linked public realm projects may follow.
findings.figures: £178k variance (FAV); delivered under budget
findings.quote: The scheme has been delivered under budget due to a number of identified risks not materialising.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: The Play Zones programme has £152k drawn down from the capital programme, and no construction start date has been confirmed.
findings.detail: The paper says three Play Zones are still at pre-construction stage, with the Rawstorne scheme progressing through design and planning. A £25k Lancashire Environmental Fund contribution supports Rawstorne, with £12.5k due in October 2026.
findings.matters: Funds have been committed to a programme that has not reached construction, and the paper says the Football Foundation timescales are still under review.
findings.figures: £152k drawdown from the Capital Programme; £18k increase in the council's contribution (April 2025 approval); £25k Lancashire Environmental Fund contribution
findings.quote: no construction start date has yet been confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Local Authority Housing Fund Phase 2 delivered 6 Afghan Resettlement units and 9 units of temporary accommodation, with a request to return the remaining funds to S106.
findings.detail: The paper states that delivery under the memorandum of understanding required 12 units, of which 4 were Afghan Resettlement units and 8 were temporary homeless accommodation. The August 2026 update requested that the remaining balance be returned to S106 monies and to Empty Homes.
findings.matters: A grant-funded housing programme with unit numbers that differ from the stated requirement, and a request to return remaining funds, is a grant-compliance point other councils running LAHF would check.
findings.figures: £146k budget (S106 and Local Authority Housing Fund); 12 units required under MoU; 6 Afghan Resettlement units and 9 temporary accommodation units delivered
findings.quote: Project delivered 6 Afghan Resettlement Units and 9 units of temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Empty Homes Strategy procurement did not appoint a partner Registered Provider, with £175k of S106 funding in place.
findings.detail: The paper says no property owners took up an offer of support. It reports that S106 funds are now targeted at one property in Kirkham, and that some empty homes need joint working with Adult Social Care and substantial investment.
findings.matters: A failed procurement route and a changed target, with the scheme now focused on one property, show a delivery model that did not proceed as planned.
findings.figures: £175k S106 Developer Contributions budget
findings.quote: Procurement unsuccessful in appointing partner Registered Provider.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Warton Village Centre's forecast contract sum is over budget, with a possible BAE contribution still to be finalised.
findings.detail: The paper says the RIBA Stage 4 design gave more accurate costs. It lists BAE funding, value engineering, or the Council funding the difference as options, and says practical completion may fall after April 2027.
findings.matters: A scheme whose forecast cost exceeds its budget and depends on an unconfirmed third-party contribution is a funding gap a finance director would need to close.
findings.figures: £299k latest budget; £4k actual expenditure to 30 September 2026; £295k variance recorded as FAV
findings.quote: Currently the forecasted Contract Sum is over the Budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Household food waste collection, funded by a £795k Defra grant, will be introduced in four phases between Autumn 2026 and Autumn 2027.
findings.detail: The paper reports national vehicle manufacturer delays, with vehicles now expected in December 2026 and further delays possible. Containers are on order, and the paper states that slippage into 2027/28 will be needed at year end.
findings.matters: The rollout timetable has moved to a four-phase plan running into 2027, and a grant-funded scheme is expected to slip into the next financial year.
findings.figures: £795k Defra grant (approved budget and latest budget); four phases; Autumn 2026 to Autumn 2027
findings.quote: it was agreed service would be introduced in 4 phases between Autumn 2026 and Autumn 2027 therefore there will be a requirement for slippage at year end.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Replacement vehicles scheme has a latest budget of £2.394m, including £1.777m slipped from 2025/26, with £1.574m spent to 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the slipped spend was needed because of long vehicle delivery lead times, and that the vehicles have now been received. It also says the scheme may need to slip again at year end if delivery timescales are delayed.
findings.matters: A large slippage figure tied to supplier lead times is a common cause of capital underspend at year end, and the paper flags the possibility of a further slip.
findings.figures: £2.394m latest budget; £1.777m slippage from 2025/26; £1.574m actual expenditure to 30 September 2026; £820k variance (FAV)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 scheme is on track, however there may be a requirement to slip at the end of the year

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital programme has a latest budget of £16.887m, with £4.059m spent to 30 September 2026 and £6.772m slipped from 2025/26.
findings.detail: The programme total shows a £278k adjustment from the Budget Council of 04/03/2026 and a £12.787m variance recorded as favourable. The total is the sum of the Portfolio schemes in the appendix.
findings.matters: Spend at the half-year point against a latest budget that includes £6.772m of slippage shows how much of the year's capital plan is still to be delivered.
findings.figures: £16.887m latest budget 2026/27; £4.059m actual expenditure to 30 September 2026; £6.772m slippage from 2025/26; £278k adjustments from Budget Council 04/03/2026; £12.787m variance (FAV)

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: The two swimming pool redevelopments have a total capital cost of £9.340m, with £2m of the £6.951m additional capital expenditure to be funded from borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says the additional expenditure is after allowing for sums already in the programme, and that £4.951m comes from the Capital Investment Reserve. It states that scheme details are still being developed and costed and will go to Executive Committee in due course.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see a new £2m borrowing requirement and a £4.951m reserve drawdown, both tied to a scheme whose costs the paper says are not yet final.
findings.figures: £9.340m total capital cost (both pools); £6.951m additional capital expenditure; £4.951m from Capital Investment Reserve; £2m from borrowing
findings.quote: The schemes required additional capital expenditure of £6.951m after allowing for sums already contained within the existing capital programme, with £4.951m being funded from the council’s Capital Investment Reserve and £2m from borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Organisational improvement spend is £3,649 at period 6 against a £15,006 budget, with the paper saying the level of spend depends on clarity about LGR
findings.detail: The paper says it is not known whether the same level of spend will be required until clarity is provided on local government reorganisation (LGR). About £6,000 of commitments have already been made for the third quarter.
findings.matters: Councils facing local government reorganisation must decide how much to hold back for transition costs, and the paper shows one council doing this.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £3,649; period 6 budget £15,006; favourable variance £11,357; full-year budget £30,000; third quarter commitments circa £6,000
findings.quote: Until clarity is provided on LGR it is not known whether the same level of spend will be required.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Splash pool entry income is £31,515 at period 6 against a £60,000 budget, which the paper says is higher than any previous year
findings.detail: The paper says income is below the budget estimate but is higher than in any previous year. The budget has been rightsized in the latest forecast.
findings.matters: A budget reset to match actual demand is a step a finance director at another council facing similar leisure income could compare against.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £31,515; period 6 budget £60,000; adverse variance £28,485; full-year budget £60,000
findings.quote: Although income is below budget estimate, it is higher than any previous year.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Kite Festival costs are £50,207 at period 6 against a £30,000 budget, while income is £11,600 against £20,000
findings.detail: The paper attributes the cost increase to greater participation from kite fliers and additional logistics. It says further income is expected from traders and expects the income to reach budget.
findings.matters: Event overspends that are not offset by income are a discretionary pressure councils run into across their festival programmes.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £50,207; period 6 budget £30,000; adverse expenditure variance £20,207; period 6 income £11,600 against £20,000 budget
findings.quote: Increased cost of delivering this event with increased participation from kite fliers and additional required logistics.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Bulk bin disposal income is £295,289 at period 6 against a £214,800 budget, following the 26/27 fee increase for trade waste customers
findings.detail: The paper links the higher income to the 26/27 Schedule of Fees and Charges, which takes account of Lancashire County Council's increased disposal charges. The forecast has been updated.
findings.matters: Trade waste fees set to pass through a upstream disposal cost increase are a pricing decision other councils would be weighing.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £295,289; period 6 budget £214,800; favourable variance £80,489
findings.quote: Increase on disposal charges to Trade Waste customers as part of 26/27 Schedule of Fees and Charges

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Other Fees for the Food Waste Collection rollout are £4,281 at period 6 against a £70,028 budget, and slippage may be required at year end
findings.detail: The paper attributes the underspend to phasing of expenditure as the food waste collection is rolled out. Printing and stationery budgets for the rollout are also underspent at period 6.
findings.matters: Slippage on a new collection service's rollout costs is a capital and revenue timing question that councils introducing food waste collections would face too.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £4,281; period 6 budget £70,028; favourable variance £65,747; full-year budget £140,000
findings.quote: Phasing of expenditure due to Food Waste Collection rollout. Slippage may be required at year end.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Planning application fee income is £539,609 at period 6 against a £426,670 budget
findings.detail: The paper says the income depends on developer confidence and other factors outside the council's control. It will be kept under review and the forecast updated.
findings.matters: Planning fee income that depends on developer confidence is a cyclical stream that other councils may also be forecasting against.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £539,609; period 6 budget £426,670; favourable variance £112,939; full-year budget £853,000
findings.quote: Application fee income and is dependent on developer confidence and other matters out of the council's control.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Employee costs are £6,668,916 at period 6 against a £6,652,216 budget, as vacancies run below the assumed saving
findings.detail: The paper says the employee budget assumes savings from vacant posts of £300k per year. It says vacancies have been slightly lower than that assumed level and that the variance is expected to reduce in the second half of the year.
findings.matters: A vacancy saving that is not being realised at the expected rate is a risk that other councils relying on similar assumptions would want to track.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £6,668,916; period 6 budget £6,652,216; adverse variance £16,700; full-year budget £12,886,888; assumed vacancy saving £300k per annum
findings.quote: The council's employee cost budget includes assumed savings from vacant posts of £300k per annum.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Emergency bed and breakfast costs are £160,825 at period 6 against a £103,342 budget, with continued homeless presentations
findings.detail: The paper says the service continues to see demand from homeless presentations, requiring emergency bed and breakfast before placement. Housing Benefit and Universal Credit income is partly offsetting the cost.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a statutory cost pressure that finance directors and lenders watch closely across councils.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £160,825; period 6 budget £103,342; adverse variance £57,483; Housing Benefit/Universal Credit income variance £28,716 favourable
findings.quote: The service still sees continued demand from homeless presentations with a requirement for emergency bed and breakfast before placement.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Cremation income is £450,619 at period 6 against a £607,410 budget, which the paper attributes to seasonal variation
findings.detail: The paper expects uplift in revenue income during quarters 3 and 4. The full-year budget is £1,214,339.
findings.matters: Cremation income is a large fee stream, and a finance director elsewhere would want to know how it is phased against the year.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £450,619; period 6 budget £607,410; adverse variance £156,791; full-year budget £1,214,339
findings.quote: Seasonal variation. Uplift in revenue income expected during Quarters 3 & 4.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Legal Services fees and court costs are £45,655 at period 6 against a £5,002 budget, with counsel opinions sought on complex matters
findings.detail: The paper says counsel opinion has been sought on a variety of more complex matters across several service areas. It states that the budget impact will be reflected in the latest financial forecast.
findings.matters: Rising external legal spend on complex matters is a cost pressure finance directors often see across several services at once.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £45,655; period 6 budget £5,002; adverse variance £40,653; full-year budget £10,000
findings.quote: The council has sought counsel opinion on a variety of more complex matters across a range of service areas.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: The closure of the swimming pool adds £587k to the Contract Management Fee across 2026/27 to 2028/29, and this is reflected in the latest forecast
findings.detail: The paper links the increase to the closure of the pool and says it has been reflected in the latest financial forecast. Legal costs on the pool contract are also recorded separately, with the paper citing the change in direction for the project and the Interim Service Agreement.
findings.matters: A multi-year fee increase from a service closure is a cost commitment that other councils running leisure contracts would need to model.
findings.figures: Additional Contract Management Fee £587k over 2026/27 to 2028/29; Contract Management Fee full-year budget £582,000; period 6 variance £88,310 favourable
findings.quote: the additional Contract Management Fee increase of £587k over 2026/27 to 2028/29 due to the closure of the pool has been reflected in the latest financial forecast.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - APPENDIX A - P6 Revenue Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Interest and investment income is £476,896 at period 6 against a £207,500 budget, which the paper attributes to the base rate and cash flow
findings.detail: The paper says the bank base rate is higher than when the budget was set, and that favourable cash flow fluctuations in the first six months allowed additional short-term investments. The full-year budget is £415,000.
findings.matters: Treasury income rising with base rate and cash flow is a source a finance director elsewhere can compare against their own investment income forecasts.
findings.figures: Period 6 actual and commitments £476,896; period 6 budget £207,500; favourable variance £269,396; full-year budget £415,000
findings.quote: The bank base rate has been at a higher rate than when the budget was set, which combined with favourable fluctuations within cash flow during the first six months

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: Construction-sector supply chain issues and price increases are described as putting increased risk on capital delivery, with UK CPI at 3.5% as at September 2026.
findings.detail: The report says inflation remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, and that the pressure is particularly strong in construction, and is likely to continue through 2026/27. Management Team will keep the position under review.
findings.matters: Cost inflation in construction feeding into scheme risk is a pressure every council with a large capital programme faces, and the paper ties it to this council's specific schemes.
findings.figures: 3.5% UK CPI year on year as at September 2026; 2% Bank of England target
findings.quote: The situation is particularly acute in the construction sector where supply chain issues and price increases have combined to put increased risks on the delivery of capital programme schemes.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: The Council is reviewing the balance between capital spend funded from earmarked reserves and from borrowing, with an updated Capital Investment Reserve and Fleet Replacement Reserve position to follow in future Financial Forecast updates.
findings.detail: The report says that, given the revenue implications of some financing options, the Council must consider the most appropriate mechanism to deliver the programme cost-effectively. The programme is shown as balanced for 2026/27 onwards, but the financing position is subject to ongoing review.
findings.matters: A council choosing between reserve funding and borrowing for a large capital programme, with reserve balances not yet updated, is a decision a finance director and a lender both need to track.
findings.quote: will be included within future updates of the Financial Forecast presented to the Executive Committee and to Council

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: Capital receipts to date total £538k, including £401k of unapplied 2025/26 receipts, against an in-year budgeted figure of £70k.
findings.detail: Receipts come from Right to Buy and general asset sales. Capital receipts are ring-fenced to fund capital expenditure, and the Council will monitor them and adjust financing in future reports.
findings.matters: Receipts well ahead of the in-year budget reduce the amount of borrowing or reserves needed to finance the programme, which affects the financing mix other councils are weighing.
findings.figures: £538k capital receipts to date; £401k unapplied 2025/26 receipts; £70k in-year budgeted figure
findings.quote: against a total in year budgeted figure of £70k

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: Vehicle replacement programme revised to a total cost of £6.447m, including 2025/26 slippage and the cost of fleet in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The Waste and Fleet team re-profiled replacement timings and updated costs, including revenue repair and maintenance as vehicles age. The financing of vehicle replacement is recorded as a risk in the Medium Term Financial Strategy, given the value involved and possible changes in vehicle costs, specifications and emissions rules.
findings.matters: A revised fleet cost with its financing flagged as a Medium Term Financial Strategy risk shows how an asset replacement cycle can move a council's capital and reserve position.
findings.figures: £6.447m total revised cost
findings.quote: with the total revised cost of £6.447m.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: Actual expenditure to 30 September 2026 is £4.059m, 24.0% of the £16.887m latest full-year capital budget.
findings.detail: The report says some schemes may be re-phased into 2027/28 once budget holders provide scheme-by-scheme information, and that this will be reflected in future Financial Forecast updates.
findings.matters: Spend at 24.0% six months into the year, with re-phasing flagged, is a measure other councils compare when judging whether their own capital programmes are slipping.
findings.figures: £4.059m actual expenditure; £16.887m latest full-year budget; 24.0% of budget
findings.quote: This equates to 24.0% of the latest budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: St Annes and Kirkham pool schemes have a total capital cost of £9.340m, with £6.951m of additional expenditure above the existing programme, and are classified as high level risks.
findings.detail: The Council approved the pool redevelopment on 27 January 2026. Of the additional £6.951m, £4.951m is funded from the Capital Investment Reserve and £2m from borrowing. Both pools are on the Strategic Risk Register because of their complexity, value, and the potential for costs beyond the approved budget.
findings.matters: A £9.340m scheme funded partly from reserves and partly from borrowing, and flagged as high risk for possible cost growth, is the kind of exposure a finance director and a lender would want to track against the approved budget.
findings.figures: £9.340m total capital cost; £6.951m additional expenditure; £4.951m from Capital Investment Reserve; £2m from borrowing
findings.quote: The total capital cost in respect of both swimming pools is £9.340m.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: The council is repeating its annual budget rightsizing exercise in 2026/27, adjusting current and future budgets for underspends over the last 3 financial years.
findings.detail: The paper describes an annual exercise the council has run for several years. It analyses underspends and adjusts budgets to better reflect resource requirements. The resulting changes will be reflected in the latest budgets and the Financial Forecast.
findings.matters: Permanently reducing budgets to match historic underspends is a specific lever to close a gap, and it changes the forecast baseline other councils and lenders would use to judge the position.
findings.figures: 3 financial years
findings.quote: analyse underspends which have occurred over the last 3 financial years and to adjust current and future year budgets

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: The Executive Committee approved £0.790m of slippage from 2025/26 into the 2026/27 budget.
findings.detail: The paper lists the slippage as one of the items in the 2025/26 outturn approval that is now reflected in the 2026/27 approved budgets. This report monitors against those updated budgets.
findings.matters: Carried-forward budget affects how far 2026/27 variances reflect in-year performance, which matters when comparing this year's monitoring with the prior year's.
findings.figures: £0.790m slippage from 2025/26
findings.quote: slippage of £0.790m from 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Position as at 30 September 2026
findings.headline: The 2025/26 revenue outturn allowed a £0.690m contribution to the Capital Investment Reserve.
findings.detail: The paper says the Executive Committee approved the 2025/26 outturn on 23 June 2026. A favourable revenue outturn, together with growth items and £0.790m of slippage, allowed the contribution to be made. The paper says this is now reflected in the ledger.
findings.matters: A reserve being rebuilt from a favourable revenue outturn is a concrete change in the council's usable reserves, and other finance directors can compare how their own outturn surpluses are being directed.
findings.figures: £0.690m contribution to the Capital Investment Reserve; £0.790m slippage from 2025/26; approval date 23rd June 2026
findings.quote: a favourable outturn position for revenue allowed for a total contribution of £0.690m to be made into the Capital Investment Reserve

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX C - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Fylde's total capital expenditure is £16,887k in 2026/27, falling to £6,193k in 2027/28 and then to £1,922k in 2028/29.
findings.detail: Spend is concentrated in 2026/27, mainly in the Tourism, Leisure & Culture Portfolio (£6,544k), the Corporate & Economic Development Portfolio (£4,227k) and the Social Wellbeing Portfolio (£2,762k). Other external finance includes a £795k Defra grant for household food waste collection and £495k from Lancashire County Council for the St Annes Pier Link project.
findings.matters: A large one-year peak in capital spend, funded partly by borrowing and reserves, is the kind of profile that affects a council's borrowing requirement and reserve position in the years that follow.
findings.figures: Total Expenditure: £16,887k (2026/27), £6,193k (2027/28), £1,922k (2028/29), £2,068k (2029/30), £4,338k (2030/31). Tourism, Leisure & Culture: £6,544k (2026/27). Corporate & Economic Development: £4,227k (2026/27). Defra grant: £795k. Lancashire County Council: £495k.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX C - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: The capital programme draws £4,549k from the Capital Investment Reserve in 2026/27 and £1,726k in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The Capital Investment Reserve is shown as a financing source for two years only. The Fleet Replacement Reserve also funds £2,394k in 2026/27 and smaller sums in later years.
findings.matters: Reserve draws reduce the cash and balances available for other uses, and a finance officer elsewhere would want to see how much of a capital programme is funded from reserves rather than borrowing or grants.
findings.quote: Capital Investment Reserve 4,549 1,726

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX C - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Fylde's updated capital programme finances £5,490k of 2026/27 spend and £2,000k of 2027/28 spend through prudential borrowing.
findings.detail: The financing summary shows prudential borrowing of £5,490k in 2026/27 and £2,000k in 2027/28, with none in 2028/29 and 2029/30. A further £2,631k is shown for 2030/31. The total surplus or shortfall in each year is shown as zero.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see the new borrowing the council plans to take on for capital schemes over the next five years, and when it is planned.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing: £5,490k (2026/27), £2,000k (2027/28), £0k (2028/29), £0k (2029/30), £2,631k (2030/31). Total surplus (-) / shortfall in year: £0k each year.
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing 5,490 2,000 0 0 2,631

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX B - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Kirkham Pool refurbishment match funding estimated at £1,500k in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: Scheme Z266 is listed as a match-funded contribution to the Kirkham Pool refurbishment, and the same £1,500k estimate appears in both years. A further £11k is listed for Kirkham Pool holding, security, preservation and project works in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Match-funding commitments of this kind depend on external or partner funding, and a finance director would want to see how the council's share is being met.
findings.quote: Z266 Kirkham Pool Refurbishment - FBC Match Fund 1,500 1,500

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX B - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: St Annes Swimming Pool improvement works estimated at £4,114k in 2026/27 and £2,226k in 2027/28
findings.detail: Scheme Z257 is the largest single item in the Tourism, Leisure & Culture portfolio, with £6,340k estimated across the two years. The portfolio subtotal for 2026/27 is £6,544k.
findings.matters: A single leisure scheme accounting for most of one portfolio's spend in two years is a concentrated commitment that other councils running similar pool projects would compare against.
findings.quote: Z257 Improvement Works to St Annes Swimming Pool 4,114 2,226

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX B - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Total capital programme estimate for 2026/27 is £16,887k, falling to £6,193k in 2027/28 and £1,922k in 2028/29
findings.detail: The updated five-year programme shows total expenditure estimates by year, with 2026/27 the highest year in the table. The paper shows estimates only, without funding sources or borrowing figures.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see how sharply the programme's spending is front-loaded into 2026/27 and 2027/28, which affects in-year cash and borrowing needs.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - St Annes Seawall - Design Development Fully Funded Budget Increase
findings.headline: The design phase does not commit the council to construction; any future build decision will require separate funding approval
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states the design work does not commit the council to the construction phase, with any future construction decision requiring a separate report, confirmation of funding, and governance approval. This represents a staged approach where the council will assess final costs and programme before deciding whether to proceed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this £400k is precursor to a much larger capital commitment; the council is explicitly retaining flexibility on the next phase.
findings.figures: £400,000 (design phase commitment only)
findings.quote: The detailed design work does not commit the Council to the future construction phase. Any future decision to proceed with construction will be subject to a separate report, confirmation of funding and approval through the Council's governance processes.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - St Annes Seawall - Design Development Fully Funded Budget Increase
findings.headline: The design phase is entirely externally funded, protecting reserves that the 2021 decision had allocated to the now-cancelled scheme
findings.detail: The 2021 decision approved £2.3m from the Funding Volatility Reserve for the original seawall scheme, phased 2021/22 to 2024/25. The new design phase is stated to be 'fully funded via the Environment Agency's Regional Area Programme Delivery Mandate', with no council capital contribution at this stage.
findings.matters: The original scheme would have materially drawn on council reserves during a period of wider financial pressure; the externally-funded design phase preserves that reserve capacity.
findings.figures: £2,300,000 (2021 reserve commitment), £400,000 (2026/27 design, EA-funded)
findings.quote: To approve a new capital scheme addition of £400,000 within the Capital Programme for 2026/27 to fund the St Annes Seawall Detailed Design Project , fully funded via the Environment Agency's Regional Area Programme Delivery Mandate.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - St Annes Seawall - Design Development Fully Funded Budget Increase
findings.headline: A seawall scheme rejected in 2023 due to cost escalation is being reactivated at design stage with a different technical approach and external funding
findings.detail: Fylde rejected a £11.82m seawall replacement project in October 2023 due to 'significant cost increases' and risk of business disruption costs. The council is now approving a £400,000 design phase for a revised approach using concrete overlay repair rather than replacement, intended to provide 100 years of protection before adaptive raising is required.
findings.matters: It shows how the council is managing a strategic coastal infrastructure challenge after an earlier project cancellation, revealing whether the asset risk has been resolved or deferred.
findings.figures: £11,820,700 (original scheme 2021), £400,000 (design phase 2026/27), 100 years (design life)
findings.quote: It was RESOLVED to not proceed with procurement and delivery of the St Annes Seawall capital scheme due to significant cost increases identified as part of the detailed design work undertaken to date, and the significant risk of potential business disruption costs exceeding their budget allocation.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - MIAA Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026
findings.headline: Limited Assurance on building statutory compliance with critical and high-priority recommendations
findings.detail: Statutory Compliance – Buildings audit finalised with Limited Assurance. Significant control gaps remain in asbestos surveys, fire risk assessments, and statutory inspection policies following the transfer of building maintenance to Blackpool Council in September 2025. The audit found incomplete records, lack of documented policies for fire, gas and electrical inspections, misalignment between service level agreements and actual inspection frequencies, and absence of performance reporting on the outsourced service. Although legionnaires testing is being completed monthly, key gaps in statutory records and inspections remain across the estate.
findings.matters: Gaps in mandatory building compliance create direct legal, financial, health-and-safety, and reputational risks; a lender needs assurance that material obligations and liabilities are being identified and managed.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance rating; 1 Critical, 1 High, 4 Medium, 1 Low recommendations; 7 remedial actions not yet due as at 9 September 2026
findings.quote: If the council does not undertake Asbestos Surveys and Fire Risk Assessments in accordance with statutory requirements, the implications are significant from a health and safety, legal, financial, operational, and reputational perspective.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - KPMG External Audit Plan and Strategy 2025-26
findings.headline: No significant risks identified in Financial Sustainability, Governance, or Economy.
findings.detail: KPMG's Value for Money assessment identified no significant risks in three domains: Financial Sustainability, Governance, and Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness. This is the auditors' initial risk assessment ahead of their full audit and opinion.
findings.matters: An external auditor's finding of no significant risks in financial sustainability and governance provides independent assurance on the council's financial management and control environment, which directly informs lender confidence in financial stability.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: no significant risks have been identified regarding the measures the council has in place for each of the three relevant domains covered by the Value for Money assessment, namely Financial Sustainability, Governance, and Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Write off of Uncollectable Debts 2025-26
findings.headline: Business rates write-off of £58,916 follows company administration triggered by large backdated valuation bill.
findings.detail: Airship Interactive Limited received a large backdated bill in February 2023 covering four years after the property was valued for the first time. Although the company paid over £50,000 under an agreed arrangement, payments ceased in May 2025 and the company entered administration in July 2025 with £1.1m in total debts (including £428k owed to HMRC). Administrators have advised that unsecured creditors (the council included) should expect no dividend payment.
findings.matters: This write-off demonstrates how large backdated valuations can precipitate business insolvencies, potentially indicating stress in the local business rates base.
findings.figures: £58,915.94 written off; company paid over £50,000 before ceasing payment; total company debts £1.1m; £428k owed to HMRC
findings.quote: This office space was not separately valued by the Valuation Office Agency until February 2023 when it was to be billed, including the prior 4 years back to 2019, which meant the ratepayer received a large, backdated bill that they could not meet in full.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Write off of Uncollectable Debts 2025-26
findings.headline: Council Tax write-offs reach seven-year high of £79,540, predominantly driven by individual insolvencies.
findings.detail: The council has written off 12 Council Tax debts totalling £79,540 in 2025-26, the highest annual value in the seven-year comparison shown. The majority result from individuals entering formal insolvency procedures (IVAs, DROs, and bankruptcy). This represents a significant increase from 2024-25 (£48,580 from 8 cases) and substantially higher than prior years (ranging from £5,100 to £37,031). While collection rates remain strong at approximately 98%, the rising volume of household insolvencies manifesting in write-offs could indicate deteriorating household financial circumstances in the area.
findings.matters: Rising Council Tax write-offs, especially those driven by household insolvency procedures, may signal weakening household finances in the area and potentially a narrowing tax base, which affects the council's revenue resilience.
findings.quote: This debt relates to an 8-year period including the current year where the taxpayer has entered an IVA. The IVA was granted in July 2025 for a total indebtedness of £19k which included Council Tax, utilities and unsecured debt.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Inflation continues to exert upward pressure on capital programme costs, particularly building and materials.
findings.detail: CPI remains at 3.4% year-on-year (December 2025) above the Bank of England 2% target. The paper specifically highlights that building costs and materials continue to rise, creating financial risks for capital programme delivery that will be a continuing issue throughout 2025/26.
findings.matters: Persistent inflation on construction costs directly impacts the adequacy of capital budgets and may require additional borrowing or reserve drawdown mid-scheme.
findings.figures: CPI at 3.4% year-on-year (December 2025)
findings.quote: This is particularly pertinent with respect to the financial risks associated with the delivery of the capital programme with building costs and materials continuing to rise. This is likely to be a continuing issue for the council throughout 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Capital programme spending is 34% of budget at December with schemes requiring slippage into 2026/27.
findings.detail: Actual expenditure to 31 December 2025 is £4.321m against a full-year budget of £12.65m, representing 34.2% spend at mid-year point. The paper indicates schemes will require slippage into 2026/27, suggesting delivery delays across the programme.
findings.matters: Programme delivery delays at mid-year can indicate wider project management, funding, or planning issues and affect planned service improvements.
findings.figures: £4.321m actual expenditure vs £12.65m budget = 34.2% spend
findings.quote: Actual expenditure to 31st December 2025 is £4.321m against the latest full year budget of £12.65m. This equates to 34.2% of the latest budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Vehicle fleet replacement financing switched from borrowing to reserve funding but flagged as a MTFS risk due to cost volatility.
findings.detail: The council has changed the financing mechanism for fleet replacement from borrowing to a dedicated Fleet Replacement Reserve. However, this change is specifically noted as a risk in the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy due to potential changes in vehicle costs, specifications and emissions regulations.
findings.matters: A switch in major capital financing away from borrowing, combined with explicit MTFS risk flagging, suggests concern about the council's ability to finance ongoing fleet replacement through reserves.
findings.figures: £4.039m revised fleet replacement cost
findings.quote: Previously, vehicle replacements have been financed from borrowing, but they are now financed from a specific 'Fleet Replacement Reserve'. The financing of vehicle replacement has been included as a risk in the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy due to the significant value of the vehicle replacement programme and the potential for changes in vehicle costs, specifications, and emissions regulations.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Swimming pools scheme classified as high-risk due to complexity, value, delivery timescales and potential for additional costs beyond budget.
findings.detail: The £9.34m swimming pools investment is explicitly classified as high-level risk. The council is funding £6.951m additional expenditure (£4.951m from Capital Investment Reserve, £2m from borrowing). The paper acknowledges ongoing possibility of additional contract costs and significant officer time requirements that may impact other council priorities before LGR vesting day.
findings.matters: A high-risk, high-value scheme requiring both reserve drawdown and new borrowing, with acknowledged cost and delivery risks, represents material financial exposure.
findings.figures: £9.34m total cost; £6.951m additional expenditure required; £4.951m from reserves; £2m from borrowing
findings.quote: The schemes require additional capital expenditure of £6.951m after allowing for sums already contained within the existing capital programme, with £4.951m being funded from the council's Capital Investment Reserve and £2m from borrowing. Due to the complexities of the scheme, its high value, the delivery timescales, and the potential for additional costs beyond those in the approved budget, the scheme is classified as a high-level risk.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: St Annes Garden Street scheme faces third-party risks that may require it to be abandoned or delayed to future years.
findings.detail: The project board has been informed of third-party risks that could jeopardise delivery. The first phase may proceed but 'the second phase may need to be aborted or delivered in future financial years'. The extent of risk will become apparent in Q1 2026.
findings.matters: Scheme abandonment or significant delay represents capital budget volatility and suggests external constraints beyond council control.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: The project board has been informed of information regarding third party risks which could jeopardise the delivery of the scheme as envisaged and require it to be delivered in two distinct phases; the first phase will follow the intended programme, but the second phase may need to be aborted or delivered in future financial years.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Capital Programme Monitoring Report – Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Kirkham Pool redevelopment cost estimates are several months old and expected to increase following site surveys.
findings.detail: The council approved a £3m estimate for reopening Kirkham Pool based on design without intrusive site survey. The paper explicitly states that revised cost estimates will take around 10 months and that 'the decision would be cognisant of the probability that the £3m capital requirement would increase'. Current estimates are several months old and the extent of increase can only be established through necessary on-site surveys.
findings.matters: A £3m+ scheme with acknowledged cost uncertainty on a complex multi-year project represents material budget risk for a council already committing significant resources.
findings.figures: £3m initial estimate; £9.34m total swimming pool investment (£6.34m St Annes, £3m Kirkham); 10-month redesign period
findings.quote: The decision to redevelop and re-open Kirkham pool will require re-design and new/revised cost estimates which will take around 10 months, the current £3m estimate is several months old and was based on a design option without on-site intrusive survey and inspection to test assumptions on the current status of the asset and the extent of required works.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 -Year-End Performance 202526
findings.headline: Council has 17 complaints overdue against a zero target, attributed to difficulty recruiting to professional statutory positions
findings.detail: The council is unable to meet its 5-day complaint-response target (17 complaints overdue vs zero target) and attributes this to 'the professional positions that continue to be difficult to recruit to'. These roles are in statutory services, so vacancies impair the council's legal compliance.
findings.matters: Persistent vacancies in statutory roles (enforcement, decision-making, audit) expose the council to legal challenge, audit findings, and inability to deliver services that generate income or protect assets.
findings.figures: 17 complaints overdue against a target of zero; last year was 74, so slight improvement but still material
findings.quote: It is the professional positions that continue to be difficult to recruit to.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 -Year-End Performance 202526
findings.headline: Council lost 59% of planning appeals against 70% target; local plan no longer current
findings.detail: The council notes that major appeals are being allowed at rates high enough to underperform its target, and attributes this to the fact that 'the current housing supply position leaves the council vulnerable to appeals that deliver housing being allowed in locations that Fylde Council would not support'. The local plan is no longer current.
findings.matters: An out-of-date local plan and inability to defend planning decisions increases risk of unplanned development, loss of planning fee income if applications are refused and appealed, and loss of control over the council's area strategy—a core plank of local governance and budget stability.
findings.figures: 59% of appeals dismissed vs 70% target
findings.quote: the current housing supply position leaves the council vulnerable to appeals that deliver housing being allowed in locations that Fylde Council would not support.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 -Year-End Performance 202526
findings.headline: Housing demand and homelessness have surged beyond budget, with 1,209 advice cases against an 800 target.
findings.detail: The council received 51% more housing advice requests than planned. Relief duty households (currently homeless) are also 16% above the 160-household budget at 186. The council attributes this to 'an increase in approaches from households at risk of homelessness, year on year', signalling a deepening affordability or employment stress in the area.
findings.matters: Sustained demand above budget for homelessness services indicates either unbudgeted pressure on reserves or the need for emergency borrowing to meet statutory duties. It also signals economic distress in the council's area, which could worsen residents' ability to pay council tax.
findings.figures: 1,209 advice cases vs 800 target; 186 relief-duty households vs 160 target
findings.quote: The service has seen an increase in approaches from households at risk of homelessness, year on year.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - App 2 - Fylde Council Strategic Risk Register July 2026
findings.headline: Unbudgeted Local Government Reorganisation transition costs of circa £620k will directly impact reserves and financial planning
findings.detail: LGR is the council's highest-scored risk (inherent 20). Specific financial consequence identified: unbudgeted transition costs estimated at circa £620k with 'potential impact on reserves and financial planning'. As of 26 June 2026, SMT was monitoring this requirement and assessing implications for reserves and budget planning through governance routes.
findings.matters: Large unbudgeted costs drawn from reserves reduce the council's financial buffer at a time of organisational transition and other pressures; this directly affects financial resilience scoring for lending decisions.
findings.figures: £620k unbudgeted transition costs; risk level 20, target 12, inherent 25
findings.quote: Financial pressure arising from unbudgeted LGR transition costs (circa £620k), with potential impact on reserves and financial planning

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - App 2 - Fylde Council Strategic Risk Register July 2026
findings.headline: Recruitment and retention challenges driven by LGR uncertainty are increasing reliance on interim staff and creating financial pressure
findings.detail: The council identifies that 'Market conditions, pay constraints and uncertainty linked to LGR are affecting the Council's ability to attract and retain staff, increasing reliance on interim resource and creating financial pressure.' This is rated as a high-risk item (16/20). No specific vacancy numbers or cost uplift is quantified in the actions.
findings.matters: Reliance on more expensive interim staff increases operating costs and reduces service continuity; key role vacancies can disrupt statutory functions.
findings.figures: Risk level 16, target 12, inherent risk 20
findings.quote: Market conditions, pay constraints and uncertainty linked to LGR are affecting the Council's ability to attract and retain staff, increasing reliance on interim resource and creating financial pressure

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Update on Risk Management and the Strategic Risk Register July 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation poses the council's highest-scoring strategic risk at 20, centred on organisational capacity constraints
findings.detail: SRR11 is Fylde's highest-scoring risk. The council identifies concerns relating to organisational capacity, engagement with transition arrangements, influence over future structures, and business as usual delivery. The reframing reflects the council's concern not with whether LGR occurs, but with whether it has the capacity to manage both transition and normal operations.
findings.matters: Suggests the council is stretched managing both routine operations and a major organisational restructuring; capacity constraints raise the risk that either transition planning or service delivery could suffer
findings.figures: current score of 20
findings.quote: The main concerns relate to organisational capacity, engagement with transition arrangements, influence over future structures, business as usual delivery and unbudgeted LGR transition costs.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Update on Risk Management and the Strategic Risk Register July 2026
findings.headline: Swimming pool capital projects remain red-rated with unresolved cost and delivery uncertainty
findings.detail: The combined strategic risk covering St Annes and Kirkham pool projects is scored at 16 (red). The risk reflects cost, programme, compliance and delivery uncertainty. Project-level risk registers are still being developed, indicating the council does not yet have cost certainty or clear delivery milestones.
findings.matters: Material capital schemes lack confirmed budgets and delivery dates; ongoing risk indicates potential for further cost escalation or timeline slippage
findings.figures: current score of 16
findings.quote: The risk remains red, with a current score of 16, reflecting cost, programme, compliance and delivery uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Update on Risk Management and the Strategic Risk Register July 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation identified as source of £620,000 in unbudgeted transition costs
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Management Group has quantified Fylde Council's estimated transition funding contribution for LGR at approximately £620,000. This has been incorporated into SRR11, the council's highest-scoring strategic risk at 20. The council identifies concerns around organisational capacity, transition engagement, influence over future structures, business as usual delivery, and these unbudgeted costs.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted costs of this scale reduce financial headroom and create cash flow pressure at a time when the council's financial stability is already under active management
findings.figures: approximately £620,000
findings.quote: The Strategic Risk Management Group discussed an estimated transition funding contribution from Fylde Council of approximately £620,000 and this has now been reflected within the risk.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: Capital programme re-financed to shift balance toward borrowing following peer review challenge on spending approach
findings.detail: The Corporate Peer Challenge (September 2024) recommended the council revisit its approach to borrowing and risk. In response, the council has re-financed the capital programme to 'optimise the balance' between reserve funding and borrowing. The direction of this rebalancing is not specified but the language suggests increased reliance on borrowing.
findings.matters: A shift toward borrowing-financed capital increases the council's debt servicing obligations and leverage. For a lender, increased borrowing changes the council's debt metrics and headroom on prudential borrowing limits.
findings.figures: Specific rebalancing amounts not detailed in this excerpt
findings.quote: the council reviewed how it finances its existing and future capital aspirations and subsequently re-financed the capital programme to optimise the balance between capital expenditure funded from the councils own earmarked reserves, and schemes financed from borrowing

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: Pay award for 2025/26 exceeded budget by 0.2 percentage points, adding cost pressure
findings.detail: The MTFS had budgeted for a 3% pay award but the actual settled rate was 3.2%. Appendix C details the adjustments this requires to employee budgets for 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: Pay awards consistently exceeding budget are a recurring pressure on councils with large workforce populations. If this becomes a pattern, it erodes the buffer within multi-year forecasts.
findings.figures: Budgeted 3%, actual 3.2%
findings.quote: The budget forecast that was approved by Council in March 2025 included an estimate for the current year pay award of 3%. The pay award has been settled at an increase of 3.2%.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: Local government unitary restructuring for Lancashire will be decided in Summer 2026 with implementation implications
findings.detail: Fylde is part of Lancashire authorities that submitted business case proposals for unitary restructuring in November 2025. The government will decide on the preferred option in Q1 2026 with parliamentary approval scheduled for Summer 2026. This could materially change the council's structure and financial arrangements.
findings.matters: Unitary restructuring carries significant risk for service continuity, financial integration, and potentially stranded assets or liabilities. For a lender, this structural uncertainty affects the council's long-term viability as a borrowing entity.
findings.figures: Consultation on preferred options beginning Q1 2026; parliamentary approval scheduled Summer 2026
findings.quote: In November 2025 Lancashire authorities submitted business case proposals to establish the best unitary structure for Lancashire. The proposals will be considered by the minister with consultation on the preferred options beginning in the first quarter of 2026. The government will decide upon which proposal for unitary councils will be implemented through parliamentary approval. This is currently scheduled to happen in Summer 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: Government funding allocations beyond 2026/27 remain unconfirmed and subject to annual change
findings.detail: Although the provisional settlement provides illustrative figures for 2026/27 to 2028/29, the council notes that these remain provisional and subject to annual confirmation. Figures for 2028/29 onwards are described as 'uncertain', with no guaranteed settlement beyond 2026/27.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed multi-year funding creates material planning risk for a five-year MTFS. The council's projected revenue surplus beyond 2027/28 depends on assumptions about funding that may change at any confirmation date.
findings.figures: Provisional figures provided for 2026/27 to 2028/29 only; years beyond described as 'a more uncertain period'
findings.quote: the settlement remains an annual event and figures for future years are subject to change until they are confirmed annually for the upcoming financial year

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus grant stream is being discontinued with no named replacement
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Local Government Finance Settlement confirms that New Homes Bonus will no longer be paid to councils. The MTFS indicates this has been incorporated into the financial forecast but no compensatory funding stream is detailed.
findings.matters: Loss of New Homes Bonus represents a material income reduction for councils. Without a replacement stream, this is a permanent gap in funding unless absorbed through other settlement allocations.
findings.figures: Discontinuation of New Homes Bonus grants
findings.quote: the discontinuation of New Homes Bonus grants

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Exec Cttee Feb MTFS
findings.headline: Discontinuation of Lancashire-wide Business Rates Pool eliminates access to pooled surplus arrangements
findings.detail: The reset to the business rates distribution methodology includes the end of the pooling arrangement that previously allowed Lancashire councils to share business rates outcomes. This removes a mechanism through which Fylde may have benefited from surplus returns in previous years.
findings.matters: Loss of Business Rates Pool membership reduces income predictability and removes the possibility of pooling gains, affecting medium-term revenue planning for a council that may have been a beneficiary.
findings.figures: Lancashire-wide Business Rates Pool discontinued for 2026/27
findings.quote: The reset to the business rates system led to the discontinuation of the Lancashire-wide Business Rates Pool for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 5- Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Council inflation provision is limited to contractual obligations only, creating exposure to price pressures
findings.detail: The council has not built in general inflation provision in its budget and limits it to areas where it has no choice due to contractual terms. With CPI at 3.4% and impact of prior years' high inflation still exerting upward pressure on utilities and supplies, the council flags that existing budget provision may be insufficient.
findings.matters: This signals vulnerability to cost pressures mid-year if suppliers or utility costs rise, and indicates the council has chosen to absorb inflation risk rather than build contingency.
findings.figures: CPI 3.4% year-on-year as at December 2025; peaked at over 11% in late 2022
findings.quote: Provision for inflation within the council's revenue budget is limited to areas where the council has no choice but to pay increased prices, e.g. due to contractual terms. Price increases represent a continuing cost pressure to the council and increases the risk that existing budget provision is insufficient to cover the cost of service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Item 5- Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Position as at 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Fylde is relying on minimum funding guarantee, indicating weaker underlying funding position
findings.detail: The council is on the minimum funding guarantee for 2025/26, meaning it did not receive an increase under the main distribution formula and is being topped up by Government. This suggests Fylde ranks below the median council in funding need by the Government's assessment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's baseline funding is structural or dependent on protection mechanisms, and minimum funding guarantee status indicates the council is in the weaker half of the funding distribution.
findings.figures: 2025/26 only; Government plans Fair Funding redistribution from 2026/27 with multiple-year allocations through 2028/29, but figures for future years remain subject to change
findings.quote: a fallback, by way of a minimum funding guarantee, for outlying councils, which for 2025/26 included Fylde council

news_drafts.headline: Fylde expects Disabled Facilities Grants to underspend by about £400k against a £2.328m budget
news_drafts.lead:
Fylde Council expects to spend about £400k less than planned on Disabled Facilities Grants by the end of 2026/27, against a budget of £2.328m. The capital monitoring report to the Internal Affairs Scrutiny Committee says: "It is expected there will be an underspend at year end of approx £400k." Actual spending on the grants stood at £657k at 30 September 2026.

The report attributes the expected underspend to competitive contractor pricing and lower-value grants. The £2.328m budget includes £713k carried forward from 2025/26. The council's Better Care Fund grant for 2026/27 is £1.535m.

The committee also had the revenue budget monitoring report, position as at 30 September 2026. It says the council is repeating its annual budget rightsizing exercise in 2026/27. The exercise, which the paper says the council has run for several years, will "analyse underspends which have occurred over the last 3 financial years and to adjust current and future year budgets". The paper says the resulting changes will be reflected in the latest budgets and in the council's Financial Forecast.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 6 - APPENDIX A - P6 Capital Monitoring Report 2026.27
